modern_osis:
Original heading

Laws concerning the priests.

Priestly holiness and the greater Priest

Israel's priests were appointed as pictures of Christ.

Ministers of the gospel should therefore imitate the Savior in their own lives, so that others may follow their example.

Christ was without blemish and separate from sinners.

He carried out his priestly work on earth in perfect holiness.

How serious, then, is the calling of anyone who ministers in his name!

Yet all Christians are spiritual priests.

Ministers are especially responsible for setting a good example, but the whole people of God should follow Christ.

Bodily weakness or disability, thank God, can no longer exclude anyone from serving him, enjoying his privileges or inheriting heavenly glory.

A healthy, beautiful soul may live within a physically weak or visibly impaired body.

And someone who is not suited to a particular form of ministry can still serve God joyfully through other responsibilities within the church.
classic_reading:
[Lev.21.1]
Chapter 21
Laws concerning the priests.
--As these priests were types of Christ, so all ministers must be followers of him, that their example may teach others to imitate the Saviour. Without blemish, and separate from sinners, He executed his priestly office on earth. What manner of persons then should his ministers be! But all are, if Christians, spiritual priests; the minister especially is called to set a good example, that the people may follow it. Our bodily infirmities, blessed be God, cannot now shut us out from his service, from these privileges, or from his heavenly glory. Many a healthful, beautiful soul is lodged in a feeble, deformed body. And those who may not be suited for the work of the ministry, may serve God with comfort in other duties in his church.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Laws concerning the priests and sacrifices.

Reverence, sincerity and trust in Christ's atonement

This chapter contains several laws about priests and sacrifices. Together they guard the honor of God's sanctuary.

We should remember gratefully that nothing can prevent our great High Priest, Christ, from performing his office.

The Lord requires us to revere his name, his truth, his appointed acts of worship and his commands.

We must beware of hypocrisy.

Let us examine ourselves for the sinful stains in our hearts and lives, seeking cleansing through Christ's blood and the sanctifying work of his Spirit.

A person who tries to atone for personal sin or approaches God proudly, relying on personal righteousness, dishonors Christ.

Such a person offends him just as seriously as someone who comes to the Lord's Table while deliberately indulging sinful desires.

A minister who loves people's souls must not allow them to remain deceived in this dangerous way.

The minister should urge them to repent of their sins and abandon them.

But repentance alone is not the whole message.

People must place their full trust in Christ's sacrifice, receiving forgiveness and acceptance with God through faith in his name.

Only in that way will the Lord make them holy as his own people.
classic_reading:
[Lev.22.1]
Chapter 22
Laws concerning the priests and sacrifices.
--In this chapter we have divers laws concerning the priests and sacrifices, all for preserving the honour of the sanctuary. Let us recollect with gratitude that our great High Priest cannot be hindered by any thing from the discharge of his office. Let us also remember, that the Lord requires us to reverence his name, his truths, his ordinances, and commandments. Let us beware of hypocrisy, and examine ourselves concerning our sinful defilements, seeking to be purified from them in the blood of Christ, and by his sanctifying Spirit. Whoever attempts to expiate his own sin, or draws near in the pride of self-righteousness, puts as great an affront on Christ, as he who comes to the Lord's table from the gratification of sinful lusts. Nor can the minister who loves the souls of the people, suffer them to continue in this dangerous delusion. He must call upon them, not only to repent of their sins, and forsake them; but to put their whole trust in the atonement of Christ, by faith in his name, for pardon and acceptance with God; thus only will the Lord make them holy, as his own people.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe feasts of the Lord, The Sabbath.1–3The Passover, The offering of first-fruits.4–14The feast of Pentecost.15–22The feast of Trumpets, The day of atonement.23–32The feast of Tabernacles.33–44
The Sabbath and appointed times (verses 1–3)

This chapter establishes holy times, including many already mentioned elsewhere.

The annual festivals brought the whole nation together at the sanctuary.

Yet even these great gatherings were no reason to give them more importance than the Sabbath.

On the Sabbath, the people were to cease from ordinary worldly work.

The rest pictured freedom from sin and the rest believers find in God.

The Lord's Sabbaths were to be observed faithfully not only in public worship but also at home, by individual families and by families gathered together.

Keeping God's Sabbath in the home would make it beautiful, strong and secure. It would help sanctify, strengthen and dignify family life.

Passover and the firstfruits (verses 4–14)

The Passover feast lasted seven days.

These were not meant to be idle days filled with games, as Henry says many people who call themselves Christians spend their religious holidays.

Offerings were made to God, and the people were to use the time for prayer, praise and godly reflection.

The sheaf of firstfruits pointed to our Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

Henry notes that Jesus rose on the very day when this offering of firstfruits was made.

The law also teaches us to honor the Lord with our possessions and the firstfruits of all our increase (Proverbs 3:9).

Israel could not eat the new grain before first offering God's portion.

We should likewise begin with God: at the beginning of every day, every meal, every undertaking and every business.

Seek God's kingdom first.

Pentecost and generosity toward the poor (verses 15–22)

The Feast of Weeks recalled the giving of the law fifty days after Israel departed from Egypt.

It also pointed ahead to the coming of the Holy Spirit fifty days after Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us.

On that day, the apostles presented to God the firstfruits of the Christian church.

The command concerning Pentecost was joined to a repeated instruction to leave gleanings in the fields for the poor.

People who truly recognize God's mercy to them will show mercy to the poor without resentment.

Trumpets and the Day of Atonement (verses 23–32)

The trumpet blasts pictured gospel preaching, summoning people to turn from sin and receive Christ's salvation.

That salvation was pictured by the Day of Atonement.

The trumpet also called the people to rejoice in God and to live as strangers and pilgrims in the world, a lesson pictured by the Feast of Tabernacles later in the same month.

At the beginning of the year, this sound urged the people to wake from spiritual laziness, examine their lives and change their ways.

The Day of Atonement followed nine days afterward.

They were given time to prepare through sincere and serious repentance so that the day might truly bring them atonement.

Humbling ourselves over sin and making peace with God require the fullest attention of both heart and mind.

On that day the Lord spoke peace to his people.

Therefore they were to set aside ordinary work so that they could hear his voice of comfort and joy more clearly.

The Feast of Tabernacles (verses 33–44)

During this feast, the people remembered their life in temporary shelters during the wilderness journey.

They also remembered how their ancestors had lived in tents in Canaan.

These memories reminded them of their origins and their deliverance.

The festival may also have pictured Christ dwelling on earth in human nature.

It certainly pictured the believer's life here: living as a stranger and pilgrim, with home and heart above, where the Savior is.

After seven days in temporary shelters, people would value the comfort of their own houses more deeply.

Those who live in ease and plenty benefit from occasionally learning what hardship feels like.

Harvest joy should make us rejoice still more in God.

Everything on earth belongs to him.

Whatever benefits we enjoy should therefore bring him glory, especially when his mercy has brought a task or season to completion.

These festivals were appointed in addition to the ordinary Sabbaths and voluntary offerings.

Extraordinary acts of service never excuse us from our regular duties.
classic_reading:
[Lev.23.1-Lev.23.3]
Chapter 23
Chapter Outline
The feasts of the Lord, The Sabbath. | (1-3) |
The Passover, The offering of first-fruits.
(4-14)
The feast of Pentecost. | (15-22) |
The feast of Trumpets, The day of atonement. | (23-32) |
The feast of Tabernacles. | (33-44) |
Verses 1-3
In this chapter we have the institution of holy times; many of which have been mentioned before. Though the yearly feasts were made more remarkable by general attendance at the sanctuary, yet these must not be observed more than the sabbath. On that day they must withdraw from all business of the world. It is a sabbath of rest, typifying spiritual rest from sin, and rest in God. God's sabbaths are to be religiously observed in every private house, by every family apart, as well as by families together, in holy assemblies. The sabbath of the Lord in our dwellings will be their beauty, strength, and safety; it will sanctify, build up, and glorify them.
[Lev.23.4-Lev.23.14]
Verses 4-14
The feast of the Passover was to continue seven days; not idle days, spent in sport, as many that are called Christians spend their holy-days. Offerings were made to the Lord at his altar; and the people were taught to employ their time in prayer, and praise, and godly meditation. The sheaf of first-fruits was typical of the Lord Jesus, who is risen from the dead as the First-fruits of them that slept. Our Lord Jesus rose from the dead on the very day that the first-fruits were offered. We are taught by this law to honour the Lord with our substance, and with the first-fruits of all our increase, [Prov.3.9] Pr 3:9. They were not to eat of their new corn, till God's part was offered to him out of it; and we must always begin with God: begin every day with him, begin every meal with him, begin every affair and business with him; seek first the kingdom of God.
[Lev.23.15-Lev.23.22]
Verses 15-22
The feast of Weeks was held in remembrance of the giving of the law, fifty days after the departure from Egypt; and looked forward to the outpouring of the Holy Ghost, fifty days after Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us. On that day the apostles presented the first-fruits of the Christian church to God. To the institution of the feast of Pentecost, is added a repetition of that law, by which they were required to leave the gleanings of their fields. Those who are truly sensible of the mercy they received from God, will show mercy to the poor without grudging.
[Lev.23.23-Lev.23.32]
Verses 23-32
the blowing of trumpets represented the preaching of the gospel, by which men are called to repent of sin, and to accept the salvation of Christ, which was signified by the day of atonement. Also it invited to rejoice in God, and become strangers and pilgrims on earth, which was denoted by the feast of Tabernacles, observed in the same month. At the beginning of the year, they were called by this sound of trumpet to shake off spiritual drowsiness, to search and try their ways, and to amend them. The day of atonement was the ninth day after this; thus they were awakened to prepare for that day, by sincere and serious repentance, that it might indeed be to them a day of atonement. The humbling of our souls for sin, and the making our peace with God, is work that requires the whole man, and the closest application of mind. On that day God spake peace to his people, and to his saints; therefore they must lay aside all their wordly business, that they might the more clearly hear that voice of joy and gladness.
[Lev.23.33-Lev.23.44]
Verses 33-44
In the feast of Tabernacles there was a remembrance of their dwelling in tents, or booths, in the wilderness, as well as their fathers dwelling in tents in Canaan; to remind them of their origin and their deliverance. Christ's tabernacling on earth in human nature, might also be prefigured. And it represents the believer's life on earth: a stranger and pilgrim here below, his home and heart are above with his Saviour. They would the more value the comforts and conveniences of their own houses, when they had been seven days dwelling in the booths. It is good for those who have ease and plenty, sometimes to learn what it is to endure hardness. The joy of harvest ought to be improved for the furtherance of our joy in God. The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof; therefore whatever we have the comfort of, he must have the glory of, especially when any mercy is perfected. God appointed these feasts, "Beside the sabbaths and your free-will offerings." Calls to extraordinary services will not excuse from constant and stated ones.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesOil for the lamps, The shew-bread.1–9The law of blasphemy, blasphemer is stoned.10–23
Oil for the lamps and the bread of the Presence (verses 1–9)

The loaves of bread in God's sanctuary represented Christ, the Bread of Life, who nourishes his people's souls.

He is also the Light of the church and of the whole world.

His light shines through his word.

By that light, we recognize the spiritual food prepared for us.

We should feed upon it in our hearts each day, and especially from Sabbath to Sabbath, with thanksgiving.

The loaves remained before the Lord in his sanctuary.

Likewise, we should remain in God's presence until he sends us on our way.

The judgment of blasphemy (verses 10–23)

The person who offended had an Egyptian father and an Israelite mother.

Henry understands the mention of both parents as illustrating the harm that can come from religiously mixed marriages.

This event led to a permanent law prescribing the stoning of blasphemers.

Scripture places serious weight on the command.

It applied to foreign residents as well as native-born Israelites.

Foreign residents were to receive the protection of the law against injustice.

They were also subject to its penalties if they broke it.

People who dishonor God's name may escape human punishment, but they cannot escape God's righteous judgment.

What hostility to God must be in the human heart when people speak blasphemies against him!

If those who rejected Moses' law died without mercy, Henry asks how much greater the judgment must be for those who scorn and misuse the gospel of God's Son.

We should guard against anger, avoid wrongdoing, refuse harmful associations with wicked people and revere the holy name that sinners dishonor.

[Lev.24.1-Lev.24.9]
Chapter 24
Chapter Outline
Oil for the lamps, The shew-bread.
(1-9)
The law of blasphemy, blasphemer is stoned. | (10-23) |
Verses 1-9
The loaves of bread typify Christ as the Bread of life, and the food of the souls of his people. He is the Light of his church, the Light of the world; in and through his word this light shines. By this light we discern the food prepared for our souls; and we should daily, but especially from sabbath to sabbath, feed thereon in our hearts with thanksgiving. And as the loaves were left in the sanctuary, so should we abide with God till he dismiss us.
[Lev.24.10-Lev.24.23]
Verses 10-23
This offender was the son of an Egyptian father, and an Israelitish mother. The notice of his parents shows the common ill effect of mixed marriages. A standing law for the stoning of blasphemers was made upon this occasion. Great stress is laid upon this law. It extends to the strangers among them, as well as to those born in the land. Strangers, as well as native Israelites, should be entitled to the benefit of the law, so as not to suffer wrong; and should be liable to the penalty of this law, in case they did wrong. If those who profane the name of God escape punishment from men, yet the Lord our God will not suffer them to escape his righteous judgments. What enmity against God must be in the heart of man, when blasphemies against God proceed out of his mouth. If he that despised Moses' law, died without mercy, of what punishment will they be worthy, who despise and abuse the gospel of the Son of God! Let us watch against anger, do no evil, avoid all connexions with wicked people, and reverence that holy name which sinners blaspheme.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe sabbath of rest for the land in the seventh year.1–7The jubilee of the fiftieth year, Oppression forbidden.8–22Redemption of the land and houses.23–34Compassion towards the poor.35–38Laws respecting bondmen, Oppression forbidden.39–55
The seventh-year rest for the land (verses 1–7)

Just as ordinary work stopped on the seventh day, the ordinary cultivation of the land was to cease during the seventh year.

These regulations warned Israel against greed.

A person's life does not consist in owning many possessions.

We should willingly depend on God's providence for our support.

We are his tenants and stewards; our possessions should be used as he directs.

The year of rest pictured the spiritual rest all believers enter through Christ.

He lifts the burden of worldly anxiety and weariness.

Our ordinary work and concerns become more bearable and more useful when they are sanctified by him.

Through Christ we are enabled and encouraged to live by faith.

The Jubilee and the prohibition of oppression (verses 8–22)

The word jubilee refers to an especially joyful sound of silver trumpets.

That sound was heard on the evening of the great Day of Atonement.

The connection showed that the proclamation of freedom and salvation through the gospel flows from the Redeemer's sacrifice.

Israelite land could not be permanently sold away from the family to which it belonged.

A sale was more like a lease lasting until the next Jubilee, when the land returned to its family.

This protected the separate identity of tribes and families until the Messiah's coming.

Likewise, anyone who had lost personal liberty could regain it at the Jubilee.

The arrangement pictured Christ's redemption from slavery to sin and Satan, and the renewed freedom of God's children.

The principle governing every sale was that no one should oppress or exploit another.

We must not take advantage of a neighbor's ignorance or desperate need.

Fear of God should restrain injustice in speech and action.

The people were promised that observing the appointed years of rest would not leave them poorer.

If we are faithful to our duty, we can entrust our needs and comfort to God.

His provision for Israel during the fallow year was a miracle intended to encourage his people in every age to trust him.

We lose nothing by faith and self-denial when we obey.

Some Israelites asked what they would eat during the seventh year.

Christians also worry about future difficulties and hesitate to follow duty because they anticipate suffering.

But we should not torment ourselves with imagined future troubles.

Our obedience may appear foolish to people concerned only with this world's interests.

Even so, the path of duty remains the path of safety.

Redemption of land and houses (verses 23–34)

If land had not been redeemed before the Jubilee, it then returned to the original seller or that person's family.

This was a picture of God's free grace in Christ.

Through that grace—not through a payment or merit of our own—we are restored to God's favor.

Houses inside walled cities were more directly the result of human labor than farmland, which was a gift of God's generosity.

A person who sold a house within such a city therefore had only one year to buy it back.

These provisions also encouraged foreigners and converts to settle among Israel.

Caring for people who have become poor (verses 35–38)

Poverty and financial decline are common sources of deep suffering.

The poor will always be among us.

We should help them by sympathy, showing genuine compassion; by service, doing practical work for them; and by material help, giving according to their needs and our ability.

We must not exploit poor people who owe us money.

The law gives two reasons to restrain oppressive lending: fear God, and help the poor remain able to live among you.

Those who struggle financially can still contribute to the community.

Rich and poor need one another.

People who have received mercy should show mercy.

Laws for debt servants (verses 39–55)

An Israelite sold into service because of debt or wrongdoing was, in the situation Henry describes, to serve six years and be released in the seventh.

Someone who sold his own labor because of poverty had to be treated in a way appropriate to a descendant of Abraham.

Masters are required to treat their servants fairly and justly (Colossians 4:1).

At the Jubilee, the servant and the servant's children were to go free and return to the family.

This pictured our redemption from slavery to sin and Satan through God's grace in Christ.

His truth makes us free (John 8:32).

We cannot buy the freedom of another sinner's soul.

But we can point people to Christ.

Through his grace, our lives can honor his gospel, express love, show thankfulness and glorify his holy name.

[Lev.25.1-Lev.25.7]
Chapter 25
Chapter Outline
The sabbath of rest for the land in the seventh year. | (1-7) |
The jubilee of the fiftieth year, Oppression forbidden. | (8-22) |
Redemption of the land and houses. | (23-34) |
Compassion towards the poor. | (35-38) |
Laws respecting bondmen, Oppression forbidden. | (39-55) |
Verses 1-7
All labour was to cease in the seventh year, as much as daily labour on the seventh day. These statues tell us to beware of covetousness, for a man's life consists not in the abundance of his possessions. We are to exercise willing dependence on God's providence for our support; to consider ourselves the Lord's tenants or stewards, and to use our possessions accordingly. This year of rest typified the spiritual rest which all believers enter into through Christ. Through Him we are eased of the burden of wordly care and labour, both being sanctified and sweetened to us; and we are enabled and encouraged to live by faith.
[Lev.25.8-Lev.25.22]
Verses 8-22
The word "jubilee" signifies a peculiarly animated sound of the silver trumpets. This sound was to be made on the evening of the great day of atonement; for the proclamation of gospel liberty and salvation results from the sacrifice of the Redeemer. It was provided that the lands should not be sold away from their families. They could only be disposed of, as it were, by leases till the year of jubilee, and then returned to the owner or his heir. This tended to preserve their tribes and families distinct, till the coming of the Messiah. The liberty every man was born to, if sold or forfeited, should return at the year of jubilee. This was typical of redemption by Christ from the slavery of sin and Satan, and of being brought again to the liberty of the children of God. All bargains ought to be made by this rule, "Ye shall not oppress one another," not take advantage of one another's ignorance or necessity, "but thou shalt fear thy God." The fear of God reigning in the heart, would restrain from doing wrong to our neighbour in word or deed. Assurance was given that they should be great gainers, by observing these years of rest. If we are careful to do our duty, we may trust God with our comfort. This was a miracle for an encouragement to all neither sowed or reaped. This was a miracle for an encouragement to all God's people, in all ages, to trust him in the way of duty. There is nothing lost by faith and self-denial in obedience. Some asked, What shall we eat the seventh year? Thus many Christians anticipate evils, questioning what they shall do, and fearing to proceed in the way of duty. But we have no right to anticipate evils, so as to distress ourselves about them. To carnal minds we may appear to act absurdly, but the path of duty is ever the path of safety.
[Lev.25.23-Lev.25.34]
Verses 23-34
If the land were not redeemed before the year of jubilee, it then returned to him that sold or mortgaged it. This was a figure of the free grace of God in Christ; by which, and not by any price or merit of our own, we are restored to the favour of God. Houses in walled cities were more the fruits of their own industry than land in the country, which was the direct gift of God's bounty; therefore if a man sold a house in a city, he might redeem it only within a year after the sale. This encouraged strangers and proselytes to come and settle among them.
[Lev.25.35-Lev.25.38]
Verses 35-38
Poverty and decay are great grievances, and very common; the poor ye have always with you. Thou shalt relieve him; by sympathy, pitying the poor; by service, doing for them; and by supply, giving to them according to their necessity, and thine ability. Poor debtors must not be oppressed. Observe the arguments here used against extortion: "Fear thy God." Relieve the poor, "that they may live with thee;" for they may be serviceable to thee. The rich can as ill spare the poor, as the poor can the rich. It becomes those that have received mercy to show mercy.
[Lev.25.39-Lev.25.55]
Verses 39-55
A native Israelite, if sold for debt, or for a crime, was to serve but six years, and to go out the seventh. If he sold himself, through poverty, both his work and his usage must be such as were fitting for a son of Abraham. Masters are required to give to their servants that which is just and equal, [Col.4.1] Col 4:1. At the year of jubilee the servant should go out free, he and his children, and should return to his own family. This typified redemption from the service of sin and Satan, by the grace of God in Christ, whose truth makes us free, [John.8.32] Joh 8:32. We cannot ransom our fellow-sinners, but we may point out Christ to them; while by his grace our lives may adorn his gospel, express our love, show our gratitude, and glorify his holy name.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesPromises upon keeping the precepts.1–13Threatenings against disobedience.14–39God promises to remember those that repent.40–46
Promises given for obedience (verses 1–13)

This chapter reinforces the laws given through Moses.

God promises rewards for obedience and warns of punishment for disobedience.

As long as Israel honored God's worship, Sabbath and sanctuary as a nation, and did not turn toward idols, the Lord promised continuing earthly benefits and religious privileges.

These promises particularly concerned life in the present world.

Yet they also pictured the spiritual blessings secured to believers through Christ in the covenant of grace.

Henry identifies seven blessings.

First, abundance. The land would produce plentiful fruit. Every good and perfect gift comes from the Father of lights.

Second, peace. God would protect his people. Those who dwell in him are safe.

Third, victory. God could save them in war whether their army was large or small.

Fourth, increase in population. In the spiritual picture, the church of the gospel would become fruitful.

Fifth, God's favor. This is the source of every real good.

Sixth, signs of God's presence through appointed worship. If we want his ordinances to remain among us, we must hold fast to them.

Seventh, the grace of the covenant. All the blessings are brought together in God's promise to be their God and make them his people.

Every covenant blessing rests upon redemption.

God had purchased Israel as his own people.

He would not cast them off until they first rejected him.

Warnings about disobedience (verses 14–39)

After the blessings God placed curses before his people.

These were warnings about what would make them miserable if they refused to obey.

Henry identifies two leading paths to ruin.

The first is despising God's commands.

People who first reject his rules may eventually reject his covenant altogether.

The second is despising God's correction.

If suffering does not teach them obedience, God himself will stand against them, which is the deepest cause of their misery.

All creation will become hostile toward them as God's judgments are sent upon them.

The warnings are detailed prophecies.

The Lord knew Israel's later rebellions and what would follow from them.

The judgments include earthly consequences.

People who refuse to part from sin when God commands them will be separated from it through his judgments.

Those who cling to their sinful desires will suffer enough from them.

The judgments also include spiritual consequences affecting the mind and conscience.

The people will find no acceptance with God and will continually be terrified by guilt.

It is just for God to leave arrogant sinners, who deliberately presume upon his mercy, without any sense of pardon.

Only free grace prevents us from wasting away under the sins into which we were born and which we have continued to commit.

God remembers those who repent (verses 40–46)

Among individuals in Israel, prosperity and suffering did not always correspond directly to a person's obedience or wrongdoing.

But the people had a unique national covenant.

Under it, national obedience was linked to national prosperity, and national disobedience brought national judgment.

Wickedness can ruin any nation, especially where God's word and the light of the gospel are available.

Sooner or later, sin brings both shame and destruction to a people.

May we humble ourselves for our sins now and turn away the approaching storm before it breaks.

May God grant that, while time remains, we attend to the things that bring lasting peace with him.
classic_reading:
[Lev.26.1-Lev.26.13]
Chapter 26
Chapter Outline
Promises upon keeping the precepts. | (1-13) |
Threatenings against disobedience. | (14-39) |
God promises to remember those that repent. | (40-46) |
Verses 1-13
This chapter contains a general enforcement of all the laws given by Moses; by promises of reward in case of obedience, on the one hand; and threatenings of punishment for disobedience, on the other. While Israel maintained a national regard to God's worship, sabbaths, and sanctuary, and did not turn aside to idolatry, the Lord engaged to continue to them temporal mercies and religious advantages. These great and precious promises, though they relate chiefly to the life which now is, were typical of the spiritual blessings made sure by the covenant of grace to all believers, through Christ. 1. Plenty and abundance of the fruits of the earth. Every good and perfect gift must be expected from above, from the Father of lights. 2. Peace under the Divine protection. Those dwell in safety, that dwell in God. 3. Victory and success in their wars. It is all one with the Lord to save by many or by few. 4. The increase of their people. The gospel church shall be fruitful. 5. The favour of God, which is the fountain of all Good. 6. Tokens of his presence in and by his ordinances. The way to have God's ordinances fixed among us, is to cleave closely to them. 7. The grace of the covenant. All covenant blessings are summed up in the covenant relation, I will be your God, and ye shall be my people; and they are all grounded upon their redemption. Having purchased them, God would own them, and never cast them off till they cast him off. ( [Lev.26.14-Lev.26.39] Le 26:14-39)
[Lev.26.14-Lev.26.39]
Verses 14-39
After God has set the blessing before them which would make them a happy people if they would be obedient, he here sets the curse before them, the evils which would make them miserable, if they were disobedient. Two things would bring ruin. 1. A contempt of God's commandments. They that reject the precept, will come at last to renounce the covenant. 2. A contempt of his corrections. If they will not learn obedience by the things they suffer, God himself would be against them; and this is the root and cause of all their misery. And also, The whole creation would be at war with them. All God's sore judgments would be sent against them. The threatenings here are very particular, they were prophecies, and He that foresaw all their rebellions, knew they would prove so. TEMPORAL judgments are threatened. Those who will not be parted from their sins by the commands of God, shall be parted from them by judgments. Those wedded to their lusts, will have enough of them. SPIRITUAL judgments are threatened, which should seize the mind. They should find no acceptance with God. A guilty conscience would be their continual terror. It is righteous with God to leave those to despair of pardon, who presume to sin; and it is owing to free grace, if we are not left to pine away in the iniquity we were born in, and have lived in.
[Lev.26.40-Lev.26.46]
Verses 40-46
Among the Israelites, persons were not always prosperous or afflicted according to their obedience or disobedience. But national prosperity was the effect of national obedience, and national judgments were brought on by national wickedness. Israel was under a peculiar covenant. National wickedness will end in the ruin of any people, especially where the word of God and the light of the gospel are enjoyed. Sooner or later, sin will be the ruin, as well as the reproach, of every people. Oh that, being humbled for our sins, we might avert the rising storm before it bursts upon us! God grant that we may, in this our day, consider the things which belong to our eternal peace.

Vows concerning persons and animals (verses 1–13)

Zeal for God's service sometimes led Israelites to dedicate themselves or their children to lifelong work in the Lord's house.

Some people could actually serve as assistants there.

In general, however, those dedicated were to be redeemed by paying a stated value.

It is good to be eager and generous in serving God.

Yet we should carefully consider the obligations we take on.

Wise judgment must guide our decisions.

Rash promises followed by reluctance to fulfill them dishonor God and disturb our own peace of mind.

Vows concerning houses and land (verses 14–25)

Our homes, land, animals and all our possessions should be used to bring glory to God.

He welcomes gifts that support his worship and advance his cause.

But the Lord does not approve of reckless generosity that leaves a person's family ruined.

Our zeal must be guided by care for those entrusted to us.

What has been fully devoted to the Lord (verses 26–33)

The law distinguishes things that were devoted to God from those that were merely consecrated.

Fully devoted things were most holy and could not be taken back or used for another purpose.

Israel was also commanded to honor God with a tenth of the produce from which it benefited, wherever that produce could be given.

In doing this, the people acknowledged him as the owner of their land and the giver of its fruit.

They confessed that they were his tenants, depending on him for everything.

They expressed gratitude for abundance already received and asked for his continuing favor.

We too are taught to honor the Lord through our possessions.

The closing word of Leviticus (verse 34)

The final verse appears to refer to the entire book.

Many of these instructions are moral laws that remain binding.

Others are ceremonial regulations given specifically to Israel.

Yet even those ceremonies have a spiritual meaning from which Christians can learn.

Through them, the gospel was proclaimed to Israel and, in this sense, to us as well (Hebrews 4:2).

The teaching that sinners are reconciled to God through a Mediator is not made clearer by the smoke of burning sacrifices.

It is made clear through knowing Jesus Christ and him crucified.

We now live under the joyful and gentle ordinances of the gospel.

True worshipers approach the Father in spirit and truth, through Christ alone and in his name.

Nevertheless, freedom from ceremonial offerings does not mean that honoring God calls for only a little thought, time or expense.

Because Jesus' blood gives us boldness to enter the Most Holy Place, let us draw near with sincere hearts and the full assurance of faith.

May we worship with greater joy and humble confidence, continually saying:

Blessed be God for Jesus Christ!

Verses 1-13
Zeal for the service of God disposed the Israelites, on some occasions, to dedicate themselves or their children to the service of the Lord, in his house for life. Some persons who thus dedicated themselves might be employed as assistants; in general they were to be redeemed for a value. It is good to be zealously affected and liberally disposed for the Lord's service; but the matter should be well weighed, and prudence should direct as to what we do; else rash vows and hesitation in doing them will dishonour God, and trouble our own minds.
[Lev.27.14-Lev.27.25]
Verses 14-25
Our houses, lands, cattle, and all our substance, must be used to the glory of God. It is acceptable to him that a portion be given to support his worship, and to promote his cause. But God would not approve such a degree of zeal as ruined a man's family.
[Lev.27.26-Lev.27.33]
Verses 26-33
Things or persons devoted, are distinguished from things or persons that were only sanctified. Devoted things were most holy to the Lord, and could neither be taken back nor applied to other purposes. Whatever productions they had the benefit, God must be honoured with the tenth of, if it could be applied. Thus they acknowledge God to be the Owner of their land, the Giver of its fruits, and themselves to be his tenants, and dependants upon him. Thus they gave him thanks for the plenty they enjoyed, and besought his favour in the continuance of it. We are taught to honour the Lord with our substance.
[Lev.27.34]
Verse 34
The last verse seems to have reference to this whole book. Many of the precepts in it are moral, and always binding; others are ceremonial, and peculiar to the Jewish nation; yet they have a spiritual meaning, and so teach us; for unto us, by these institutions, is the gospel preached, as well as unto them, [Heb.4.2] He 4:2. The doctrine of reconciliation to God by a Mediator, is not clouded with the smoke of burning sacrifice, but cleared by the knowledge of Christ and him crucified. We are under the sweet and easy institutions of the gospel, which pronounces those true worshippers, who worship the Father in spirit and truth, by Christ only, and in his name. Yet, let us not think, because we are not tied to the ceremonial rites and oblations, that a little care, time, and expense, will serve to honour God with. Having boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, let us draw near with a true heart, and in full assurance of faith, worshipping God with the more cheerfulness and humble confidence, still saying, BLESSED BE GOD FOR JESUS CHRIST.
